title: K-flatness and scalar-extension projectivity for bounded ring complexes
statement: Let $\varphi:A\to B$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings. Regard modules as sheaves on their one-object bottom-topology sites [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. Let $F$ be an additive functor from $A$-module sheaves to $B$-module sheaves with $F(M)=M\otimes_A B$ given by the shared sheafified change-of-rings construction [def-pur-sheaf-tensor-product]. Let $P$ be a cochain complex of these $A$-module sheaves, with integers $a,b$ such that $P^n$ is zero for $n<a$ or $n>b$, and suppose each evaluated $A$-module $P^n(*)$ is projective (linear maps from it lift through surjective linear maps). Then $P$ is K-flat [def-pc-kflat-complex], and every evaluated term $F(P^n)(*)$ of termwise scalar extension is a projective $B$-module. No finite-generation hypothesis on the terms or flatness hypothesis on $\varphi$ is needed.

proof.text: Evaluation at the unique object, with inverse constant presheaf, identifies module sheaves with ordinary modules. There is no nonidentity restriction map and the bottom topology imposes no extra condition. The same holds on its slice. Evaluation identifies the shared sheafified tensor with ordinary tensor: sheafification is the identity up to its unit on this site. It identifies total tensor complexes termwise, including their differentials and acyclicity.

Each projective module is a retract of a free module, hence flat. The given upper bound makes the evaluated complex bounded above. Apply the bounded-above flat module theorem to each evaluated acyclic complex. The tensor identification from the first step and reflection of acyclicity give the shared K-flat predicate.

For every projective term choose a splitting P^n(*)→A^(I)→P^n(*) whose composite is the identity. Tensor the two maps with B; functoriality preserves their composite. Since B⊗_A A^(I)=B^(I), the extended term is a retract of a free B-module and is projective. The specified object equalities for F and the tensor identification of step one identify it with F(P^n)(*). This works for arbitrary ranks, zero rings and zero terms, with no flatness assumption on B over A.
